Threshold or deblur an image to binarize features

Source: R/LilHelpers3.R
image_threshold.Rd

Turns a grayscale image into a binary one, either against a single image-wide level (method = "global") or against the local brightness around each pixel (method = "adaptive"). A separate deblur = TRUE mode instead separates two layers of a segmented image.

Usage

image_threshold(
  img,
  threshold = 0.4,
  method = "global",
  adaptive_k = 1.15,
  window_size = 51,
  select_layer = 2,
  mask_layer = 1,
  binary_01 = FALSE,
  deblur = FALSE
)

Arguments

img

SpatRaster object.

threshold

Fraction of the global maximum, between 0 and 1, used by method = "global" and by deblur = TRUE. Not used by method = "adaptive", which takes adaptive_k instead.

method

"global" or "adaptive". Ignored when deblur = TRUE.

adaptive_k

Multiple of the local mean a pixel must reach to count as foreground, for method = "adaptive" only. Must be above 1 for the method to separate anything; see the section above.

window_size

Odd integer, the side of the local-mean box in pixels, for method = "adaptive" only.

select_layer

Integer or NULL. Which layer to threshold or deblur. If NULL and the image is multilayer, the mean of all layers is used.

mask_layer

Integer or NULL. If set, this layer is thresholded against its own level rather than against select_layer's.

binary_01

Logical. If TRUE, the output is 0/1; if FALSE, it keeps the maximum value of the input.

deblur

Logical. If TRUE, runs the deblurring mode instead of thresholding.

Value

SpatRaster object.

Global thresholding

A pixel is foreground when it is at least threshold times the brightest value in the image. One level for the whole image, so it only works when the illumination is even: a flatbed scan with a bright center and dark corners has no single level that is right everywhere.

Adaptive thresholding

A pixel is foreground when it is at least adaptive_k times the mean of the window_size x window_size box around it. The reference level follows the illumination, so a brightness gradient leaves the decision unchanged.

Two constraints decide whether it works, and both are properties of the image rather than preferences:

adaptive_k must exceed 1. In a window holding only background the local mean is the background level, so background pixels sit on both sides of it. At adaptive_k = 1 half of a root-free patch comes out as root; below 1 nearly all of it does. The margin needed above 1 scales with the background noise: on test images with a background coefficient of variation of 5%, adaptive_k = 1.15 leaves 0.1% of a root-free patch marked, while 1.05 leaves 16%. The useful range runs from roughly 1 + 3 * cv up to the root-to-background brightness ratio; past that ratio the roots fail their own test and nothing is found. Across test images spanning root/background contrasts of 1.3 to 2.2 and background CVs of 2% to 10%, the best value fell between 1.10 and 1.20.

window_size must be large compared with the widest root. The window average includes the root itself, so a root that fills much of its own window raises its own reference level and is rejected. With roots up to 9 px wide, F1 against a known mask rose from 0.54 at window_size = 15 to 0.90 at 51 and 0.96 at 101, and the useful adaptive_k rose with it, from 1.05 to 1.20, as the reference level stopped being contaminated. A window about ten times the widest root is a reasonable starting point; there is no penalty for going well beyond that, because the cost is flat in window_size and the reference level still tracked an eightfold illumination gradient at window_size = 151.

What neither method can do

Both methods mark pixels that are brighter than a reference, so they separate bright features on a darker background and nothing else. Where root and soil have the same brightness, no threshold of either kind can tell them apart, and the useful range for adaptive_k described above is empty: its lower bound sits above its upper bound. The bundled minirhizotron scan is such an image. Measured against the matching segmentation, its roots average 1.07 times the soil brightness, while the soil's own coefficient of variation runs from 0.23 to 0.93 across the frame – the soil texture varies several times more than root differs from soil – and adaptive thresholding reaches an F1 of about 0.1 there. That is a property of the image rather than of the implementation. Scans like it need a trained segmenter such as RootDetector, whose binary output the rest of Rootopia reads directly.

Deblurring

deblur = TRUE ignores method. It subtracts select_layer from mask_layer and thresholds both at threshold times the maximum of select_layer, which separates in-focus structure from an out-of-focus halo in a two-layer segmented image.

Examples

img = terra::rast(seg_Oulanka2023_Session03_T067)
image_threshold(img, threshold = 0.3, method = "global")
#> class       : SpatRaster
#> size        : 1161, 4900, 3  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
#> resolution  : 1, 1  (x, y)
#> extent      : 0, 4900, 0, 1161  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#> coord. ref. : 
#> source(s)   : memory
#> names       : lyr.1, lyr.2, lyr.2
#> min values  :     0,     0,     0
#> max values  :   255,   255,   255
image_threshold(img, threshold = 0.4, select_layer = 2, mask_layer = 1, deblur = TRUE)
#> class       : SpatRaster
#> size        : 1161, 4900, 3  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
#> resolution  : 1, 1  (x, y)
#> extent      : 0, 4900, 0, 1161  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#> coord. ref. : 
#> source(s)   : memory
#> names       : lyr.1, lyr.2, lyr.2
#> min values  :     0,     0,     0
#> max values  :   255,   255,   255

# Adaptive thresholding, on a small image that meets both conditions above:
# the background falls from 0.40 to 0.11 across the frame, a 3.6-fold range
# no single global level can follow, and three 1 px roots sit at twice their
# own local background. The window is far wider than the roots, and the
# multiplier is above 1.
m <- outer(seq(1, 0.4, length.out = 120), seq(1, 0.7, length.out = 120)) * 0.4
m[, c(20, 50, 90)] <- m[, c(20, 50, 90)] * 2
bw <- image_threshold(terra::rast(m), method = "adaptive",
                      adaptive_k = 1.15, window_size = 31, binary_01 = TRUE)
terra::plot(bw)
